# Filtering searches by file type

By default `rg` looks in every file under the directory you run it in. When you
only care about one kind of file, the type filters cut the rest away. They are
a naming shortcut: instead of remembering that C code lives in both `.c` and
`.h` files and writing `rg 'int main' -g '*.{c,h}'`, you write
`rg 'int main' -tc`.

## Seeing what is on offer: `--type-list`

ripgrep ships with a long list of predefined types, covering well known public
formats. To see them:

```
$ rg --type-list
```

Each line is a type name, a colon, then the comma-separated filename patterns
that belong to it:

```
$ rg --type-list | rg '^make:'
make: *.mak, *.mk, GNUmakefile, Gnumakefile, Makefile, gnumakefile, makefile
```

Some formats answer to more than one name: `markdown` and `md` appear as
separate lines with identical patterns, and either one works. The list also
takes into account any types you define on the same command line, so it doubles
as a way to check that a definition of your own came out the way you meant.

## Searching only one kind of file: `--type` (`-t`)

```
$ rg 'fn run' --type rust
$ rg 'fn run' -t rust
$ rg 'fn run' -trust
```

All three are the same command; the short form may be written with or without a
space. Repeat the flag to widen the net, and the types add up:

```
$ rg invoice -tmd -tjson -tcsv
```

Once you have used `-t` even once, any file matching none of your chosen types
is skipped. Ask for a name ripgrep does not know and it stops with
`unrecognized file type: ...` rather than quietly searching everything.

## Leaving one kind out: `--type-not` (`-T`)

The mirror image. `-t` means "include files of this type", `-T` means "exclude
files of this type":

```
$ rg clap --type-not rust
$ rg clap -Trust
```

It repeats too, and it mixes freely with `-t`. If a single file matches both an
included and an excluded type, the flag written **last** on the command line
decides.

## The special name `all`

`--type all` behaves as though you had asked for every type in `--type-list` at
once, including any you defined yourself. The effect is that ripgrep searches
only files it recognises and ignores everything else.

`--type-not all` is the opposite, and searches only the files ripgrep does
*not* recognise.

Suppose you have a shell script named `my-shell-script`, with no extension,
sitting beside `my-shell-library.bash`. Both `-tsh` and `-tall` find matches
only in `my-shell-library.bash`, because the `sh` patterns do not cover
extensionless names. `-Tall` finds matches only in `my-shell-script`.

## Defining your own: `--type-add`

If you keep reaching for the same set of extensions, give it a name. The value
is a type name, a colon, and one filename pattern:

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.html' --type-add 'web:*.css' --type-add 'web:*.js' -tweb title
```

Only one pattern per flag, but repeats accumulate, and a pattern can list
several extensions in braces, so this is the same thing more briefly:

```
$ rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' -tweb title
```

Your patterns are added to ripgrep's built-in ones rather than replacing them.
Type names must consist only of letters and numbers, with no punctuation, and
`all` is reserved.

You can also build a type out of types that already exist, using `include`
followed by a comma-separated list:

```
$ rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md' -tsrc TODO
```

and then layer extra patterns on top of it:

```
$ rg --type-add 'src:include:cpp,py,md' --type-add 'src:*.foo' -tsrc TODO
```

Everything named after `include:` must already be defined at that point, so put
your own `--type-add` flags before the one that includes them. (A related flag,
`--type-clear NAME`, throws away a type's existing patterns, which is how you
start from scratch rather than adding to what is there.)

Definitions last for the one command only; nothing is saved anywhere. To keep a
type around, either make a shell alias:

```
alias rg="rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}'"
```

or put a line in your configuration file, the one `RIPGREP_CONFIG_PATH` points
at:

```
--type-add=web:*.{html,css,js}
```

## Three things that catch people out

- **Patterns match a file's name, not its location.** `*.txt` works;
  `drafts/*.txt` will never match anything, because only the last part of the
  path is tested. To filter on where a file sits, use `-g`/`--glob` instead.
- **Files you name yourself are always searched.** In
  `rg -trust TODO notes.txt`, `notes.txt` is searched anyway. Type filters
  apply to the files ripgrep goes looking for, not to paths you hand it
  directly.
- **Types lose to globs and to ignore files.** `-g` patterns and the rules in
  `.gitignore` and its relatives are applied first, and a `-t` cannot pull back
  a file they have already excluded.
